docTitle: Is your API returning the right HTTP status code?

slides.title: Is your API returning the *right* HTTP status code?
slides.sub: The codes I use in real APIs, and the mistakes I see most.

slides.title: Your front end and your monitoring read the *status code* first
slides.body: The code tells them what happened, and the body gives the detail. If the code is wrong, everything that reads it is wrong too.

slides.title: The first digit tells you which class it is

calls.nm: OK, with the book in the body
Created, usually with a Location header

slides.title: Which redirect? 301, 302, 307 or 308
slides.body: With 301 and 302 a POST can turn into a GET, and the data you sent is dropped. If POST requests matter, I would use 307 and 308.

slides.title: 400 or 422?

cols.v: The server can't read the request, like broken JSON
The JSON is valid. The data inside makes no sense

slides.body: I think 422 is clearer for validation, because it tells the front end that the format was fine and the data is what needs fixing.

slides.title: 401 and 403 lead to different screens

cols.v: Send the user to log in or refresh their token
Show a message that they don't have access

slides.body: If you return 403 for an expired token, your front end never sends the user back to log in, and they are just stuck.

slides.title: GitHub hides private repos behind a 404

shot.credit: GitHub Docs, Troubleshooting the REST API

slides.body: RFC 9110 allows this too, as a way to avoid confirming that private resources exist.

slides.title: Your app sends 500. The proxy sends 502 and 504

calls.nm: The proxy got an invalid answer from your app
Your app took too long, like a slow query

slides.title: 4 common status code mistakes
rows: Returning *200 OK* when the request failed
A 500 for a record that doesn't exist, instead of a 404
A 403 for an expired token, instead of a 401
Leaking stack traces in your 500 responses
